item.title: A New 'Now Moment': The Joys of Things Unpresent
item.description:
Meditation

A New 'Now Moment': The Joys of Things Unpresent

Positive anticipations optimize a future of our own making and our own design.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • We often "pre-enjoy" future events and activities before we actually experience them.
  • Now moments enriched by positive anticipation nourish us in ways actual experience often doesn't.
  • Optimism is a potent expectation fed by hope-filled pre-constructions of experiences yet to come.

Rather than waiting for a much-anticipated event or activity to unspool in real time, we often enjoy it before we actually experience it. By bringing to mind pleasantly edited images of the activity we are yet to experience, we preview it favorably, pre-sampling the joys the activity is expected to bring us.

"I’m looking forward to it!" This is the well-worn expression used to describe our mental musings about a hope-filled, unexperienced future, musings that sprinkle a savory seasoning over our current moment, enriching it.

The Very Mortal 'Now Moment'

Our moments are always fleeting "passing" ones. But despite their brief mortality, the powerful pleasure hormone, dopamine, surges to its highest levels in those pivotal moments of anticipation when a longed-for future experience is expected to bring us big rewards.

It’s in the absence of the actual experience that we fire up the engine of joyful anticipation, causing it to roar. Indeed, the most rewarding part of our longed-for experience often comes in a version birthed in our imagination, its anticipated form. Here, a well-orchestrated effort takes place among the shared neurocircuitries of the prefrontal cortex or the executive brain and the endogenous reward system—"the organs of anticipation."

Such positively charged anticipations saturate our now moment with a mentally pre-lived, optimized future of our own making, our own design. These fantasized versions of reality then grant our every wish indiscriminately. This can drive our motivation even overcome any future obstacles.

And when the future does arrive, we feel we’re on familiar soil, more at home, because we are primed and ready to respond in accordance with our prior, positive anticipations. We are therefore predisposed to interpret or shape the meanings of the realities about to unfold before us.

Imagined Joys vs. Real Ones

Ironically, there are times we find less joy, even disappointment, in our activities when they are actually lived than when they were merely anticipated or pre-experienced imaginatively. Greater enjoyment came during those coveted moments when longing for the activity heavily invested it with anticipatory excitement and hopefulness.

Moreover, our positive anticipations often set a high standard unmatched by our actual experience.

Pre-Editing Our Future Experiences

Our optimistic expectations pre-edit our future activities, crafting them into their ideal form, thus foreclosing upon their real-life downside. Inconveniences, discomforts, and miscellaneous encumbrances typically crop up as we navigate the complicated realities that regularly accompany our actual life experiences.

article continues after advertisement

What often plays out in real life as lackluster, or little more than ordinary experience, was extraordinary as we imagined how it might be when we pre-lived it idyllically. Our optimistic now moment nourished us in a manner that actual experience didn't, couldn’t or wouldn't.

The Conventional Now Moment

The conventional now moment accessed or achieved by mindfulness and meditation promises us science-supported, across-the-board health benefits, stretching broadly from enhanced immune function to heart and brain health. A recent Harvard study found evidence of significant increases in gray matter density and improved cognitive function in those who practiced just eight to 10 minutes of daily mindfulness meditation.

Mindfulness helps fasten us to a now moment emptied of unsettling, stress-inducing contaminants, the psychological debris of past worries and future apprehensions. Freed of these, we inhabit a serene, peaceful moment of tranquility unleashed from self-recrimination, judgmentalism, and other non-acceptance.

We find an "anchor," typically in focused breathing, that tunes us exquisitely to the sensations arising from within ourselves which imparts a healthy detachment from extraneous, outside preoccupations, thus conferring profound feelings of well-being.

Because of these wide-ranging benefits, mindfulness meditation should take its rightful, secured and well-practiced place within our repertoire of daily self-care habits.

article continues after advertisement

A Caveat: An Omnipresent Now

Three months prior to Albert Einstein’s death, he received a letter from a recently deceased friend’s widow. In her letter, the widow made a reference to their past friendship to which Einstein responded with this cryptic, mind-boggling comment, "...the distinction between the past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion."

Unfortunately, Einstein himself deceased shortly after making his provocative statement and was not able to fully explain what he had meant. But if Einstein was right, as he often was, maybe our past, present, and future moments are indistinguishable, the sheer artifact of our brain’s delimited, perceptual apparatus.

Perhaps our now moments can never be fully purged of the influences of our past, present, or future because they are all the same moment. As per Einstein’s postulations, maybe we inhabit an omnipresent moment, one that has no beginning or end.

What are your now moments like? What would you like them to be?

item.title: In Memoriam: Isaac Prilleltensky
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

In Memoriam: Isaac Prilleltensky

The legacy of Isaac Prilleltensky, a critical theorist and well-being scholar.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Prilleltensky's legacy has changed and can still change how we promote well-being in daily life and policy.
  • His legacy encourages us to focus on bottom-up community interventions, where more voices are included.
  • His legacy reminds us that we need to align with human values if we want the promotion of well-being to work.

May 7, 2026. I was finding my way into the crowds at Dublin Airport, rushed by the weight of the kilted bag in my hurt hand and the pace of the passersby. As I checked my phone to trace the gate number, a text message poured freezing water into my heart: “Dear friend! I have sad news! Isaac P passed away yesterday,” said Ottar Ness.

Isaac Prilleltensky held a guest professorship position at NTNU, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, my alma mater, and the institution where I had just returned to work part-time, highly motivated to continue my work and mentorship with him and Ottar. I knew he was unwell, yet the resilient tone in our last email made me fall into the fallacy that all those whom we admire are immortal. And they are, somehow; may their legacy stay alive in us.

Isaac changed the lives and work of academics worldwide by challenging us to comprehend well-being in the light of power dynamics and social justice. For instance, he encouraged well-being researchers to focus on SPEC—strengths, prevention, empowerment, and community change[1]—transforming how well-being interventions are designed, evaluated, and translated into policy. In collaboration with NTNU WellFare, his ideas even inspired the World Health Organization's work on well-being economies[2].

Whether you have heard of Isaac Prilleltensky or not, he might have already had an impact on the ways well-being is promoted in your city or your country, without you even having been aware of it. He can still change your life for the better, or even encourage you to become a changemaker, if you dare to get closer to his legacy. There are at least three ways in which his work might have made or can make your life more meaningful.

He dared to challenge mainstream systems, and so could you

Isaac Prilleltensky was not only a community psychologist but also a critical theorist[3]. He advocated for more voices to be heard in the decisions that matter to the personal, relational, and collective dimensions of their everyday lives[4]. As obvious as it sounds, the idea of being heard prior to others making decisions that affect us is an approach that opposes some of the premises many "experts" still stand by, comfortably supporting top-down decisions that leave contextual richness at the doorstep of university labs. In contrast, Isaac’s legacy has made it easier for policymakers and research boards to understand why we need continuous user experience and systemic comprehension of everyday life contexts when planning, executing, or assessing community interventions.

He wanted human values at the core—which ones matter the most for you?

Isaac Prilleltensky’s approach to community psychology is an invitation to lift the conversation about ethics and morals when promoting well-being. A values-based approach to well-being is far from toxic positivity stances that idealize harmony and joy; it requires us to point at conflicting values in processes and decisions, incongruences in what is preached but not lived through, and the humility to begin anew and strive for a sense of personal and collective congruence as we build up, together, societies where the common good is promoted from the inside out. Bringing values to the core of it all calls for awareness, and awareness sparks with critical questions that invite us out of our comfort zones.

article continues after advertisement

He brought common sense to the core of well-being

Isaac Prilleltensky wanted to make common sense a common practice in the ways we think and do psychology. He reminds us that we all deserve a good life. However, not all of us have the same opportunities to achieve such a sense of well-being, and we can also disagree upon what a good life is about and how to achieve it. Prilleltensky’s work revolves around three words that simplify the understanding of, and thus also the tasks involved in, promoting well-being: mattering, wellness, and fairness[5].

In a nutshell, to experience well-being, we need to feel that we matter to others, that we have a place around the table where we can actively contribute, and where our contributions are appreciated and included[6]. Then, we also need to perceive that the positives count more than the negatives in our lives, that our emotional bank account of joyful experiences is not emptied out by instances of suffering that outweigh them[7]. Then, we need to experience fairness, a sense of justice in the ways we are treated, and a belief that power structures can be challenged democratically so that there is consciousness of the privileges and disadvantages of community members, and that the common good is fostered inclusively[8].

Whenever I find myself in days of struggle, making sense of moral injuries in our politics, or in the very perils of being an academic in times like ours, I find counsel in Isaac’s work, asking myself: Where do I feel I matter as a person? What gives me wellness? Where am I treated fairly?

And vice versa: In which areas of my life have people intended to make me feel an outsider and dismissed my input? Where, in my life, do I feel exhaustion? What makes me suffer and steals my opportunities for joy? And what are the injustices that hurt me the most?

These questions have helped me gain clarity about my moral compass and the values I want to align with in my daily life. These or similar questions might help you strive for personal, relational, and collective actions that are congruent with the human values that most matter to you. This was Isaac's hope for us to achieve, one daily practice of social justice at a time, the common good we all know is possible.

article continues after advertisement

Acknowledgments: Thanks to Ottar Ness for his feedback and contribution in shaping this text, as we mourn together the loss of a dear colleague and mentor.

item.title: Event, Response, Outcome: A New Lens on Addiction
item.description:
Addiction

Event, Response, Outcome: A New Lens on Addiction

A path to reclaiming agency from alcohol misuse without blame or shame.

Posted July 26, 2026

For years, I uttered the same line to myself with a tone that resembled self-hatred every time I faced another negative consequence from my drinking: "You did this to yourself."

Whether it was missing work after a night of heavy drinking, an ultimatum from a loved one, or a bad fight with my boyfriend after the second bottle of wine, the same line would echo in my head as I sat with the consequences.

So when I walked out of Zuckerberg San Francisco General Hospital with a diagnosis of Alcohol Use Disorder in my hand, for a moment, I felt relieved. Finally, there was an explanation for my behavior—it was not all my fault.

But the relief only lasted a moment before another feeling crept in: powerlessness.

When it was all my fault, at least I could do something about it. But if it was not my fault, then did it also mean that there was nothing I could do about it?

For years, I felt as if I was forced to choose between two equally dreadful options: staying in self-blame or forfeiting my power.

Two Incomplete Stories About Addiction

We have been told different stories about addiction. Once upon a time, there was the story of blame. We believed that addiction was about weak character, moral failure, and ultimately, bad choices. Over time, our understanding evolved, and we began to call it a disease.

The new narrative offered a much more compassionate view of those who struggle; however, it also came with an unintended implication: it could undermine a person's sense of agency and dampen hope for healing beyond the diagnosis. Addiction became a condition that could be managed but not cured, and an identity that, while often adopted with the intention of reducing shame, unmistakably came to define the person who carried the diagnosis.

The old story assumed that a person had complete control over their choices, while the new story suggested that they had none at all. For a long time, like many people in my position, I felt that I had to choose between compassion and agency.

Until a deceptively simple formula offered me a third path.

A Third Path: Event + Response = Outcome

I encountered this formula while I was undergoing my training to become a therapist: Event + Response = Outcome.

The formula states that the life we live today is the outcome of what happens in our lives (events) plus how we respond to those events (responses). It points out that while we can't change the events, we have the power to change our responses and, therefore, the outcome.

At first glance, this almost seemed like a reiteration of the old "You did this to yourself" narrative. But my therapist training allowed me to see something that was left unspoken in the formula: before our responses began shaping our lives, they were first shaped by our life experiences.

None of us are born with healthy and effective ways to respond to the pain and difficulties that are inherent in life. We learn them through loving, well-adjusted adults who model them for us. And when those figures are unavailable or absent during our years of development, we adapt whatever responses are available to help us cope. For me, one of those responses was drinking.

When we fully grasp that our responses are first shaped by our experiences and our environment, it becomes possible to shift away from blaming ourselves for everything that has happened in our lives.

But here's the equally important part: while many of our current responses were developed outside our awareness—and often out of necessity—once we become aware of them, we have the opportunity to develop new capacities and choose different responses.

article continues after advertisement

If drinking became one of the responses we learned to life's challenges, then healing is not simply about removing alcohol. It is about expanding our capacity to respond differently.

In other words, while our past explains our present, it doesn't have to dictate our future.

Event + Response = Outcome
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

When Drinking Becomes Automatic

For most seasoned drinkers, drinking eventually becomes a default response for coping with pain, discomfort, and life's challenges. From stress to unwanted feelings, from boredom to intimidating tasks, it often becomes the go-to response before our thinking brain can fully engage.

When drinking becomes our automatic response, it often stops being a conscious choice every time we pick up a drink, becoming more of a default strategy for responding to life. I call this Automated Routines, one of the invisible forces that keeps people stuck in what I came to call the Invisible Drinking Loop.

To break a well-practiced drinking routine takes more than just removing alcohol, and it isn't as simple as replacing one behavior with another. It requires expanding our capacity to respond to life's challenges emotionally, mentally, and behaviorally. I call this process of developing new ways to respond Skill Expansion. It’s one of the Four Pillars of outgrowing an outdated drinking pattern and rebuilding self-trust beyond alcohol.

The First Step Toward Change

Before we can expand our responses, we first have to become aware of the invisible forces shaping our current ones. If our drinking is an automatic response rather than simply a bad choice, then trying to change it without understanding what's driving it is like treating the symptom while ignoring the cause.

Only when we recognize the invisible forces that have been shaping our current drinking pattern can we develop new responses to life's challenges instead of repeating our old drinking patterns. Awareness is the first step toward creating lasting change and reclaiming our agency.

item.title: Why Workaholics May Not Be Team Players
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Why Workaholics May Not Be Team Players

Balancing task focus with helping behaviors in the workplace.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Workaholics tend to take on unnecessary work at the expense of teamwork.
  • Work "addiction" is a dispositional investment in work responsibilities instead of relationships.
  • Workaholics function best in autonomous, specialized jobs rather than collaborative projects.
  • Workaholism decreases investment in prosocial organizational citizenship behavior.

We all know someone we would characterize as a workaholic. In fact, many of these people self-identify as such. Although we view hard workers as valuable producers, there are other factors to consider. A quantity over quality mindset creates the possibility of mistakes, and “all work and no play” is a recipe for burnout. So, where do we draw the line?

Source: Image by Daria Nepriakhina from Pixabay

Quantity Over Quality: A Question of Perception

Guido Alessandri et al. (2020) examined workaholism in a piece entitled “The Costs of Working Too Hard.”[i] They started by recognizing that although hard work yielding achievement is an intuitive link, research tends to depict workaholics as hard workers rather than smart workers.

Alessandri et al. define workaholism or work addiction as “a dispositional type of heavy work investment” causing employees to feel obligated to work and engage in work-related activities driven by internal forces that control their behavior.

They point out something many of us have noticed in our colleagues and perhaps ourselves: Workaholics tend to work beyond what is reasonably expected or requested, displaying a “compulsive and obsessive” preoccupation toward their work. The question for organizations is how does this disposition impact office productivity and culture?

Putting Job Responsibilities Over Relationships

Alessandri et al. examined the link between workaholism and prosocial organizational citizenship behavior (P-OCB), which represents individual behavior that is “discretionary, not directly or explicitly recognized by the formal reward system,” and promotes effective and efficient organizational functioning. They note that P-OCB is characterized by displaying positive, personal interest in coworkers and colleagues, and constructive behavior such as helping others who have been absent. This disposition benefits other employees as well as the organization as a whole by promoting a higher level of productivity, better allocation of resources and flexibility, and a higher degree of performance stability.

Following a sample of 85 police officers for three months, Alessandri et al. found that workaholic tendencies negatively predicted P-OCB indirectly through an employee’s perception of job requirements. They observe that workaholics perceive and actively seek out job demands which decrease P-OCB.

Hard Work and Team Playing

article continues after advertisement

Alessandri et al. recognize their results question the popular belief that hard work naturally makes workaholics good performers—although this is sometimes true. They note that working hard often leads to producing more, although excessive performance may be counteracted by decreased contextual job performance. Subsequent research has also shown that workaholism and related dimensions have different types of impact on different aspects of work performance.[ii]

Regarding whether workaholics are a good investment for an organization, Alessandri et al. suggest that it depends on the job they are hired to do. The ideal niche for a workaholic is a job characterized by a high degree of complexity and competency, as well as jobs where performance does not require employee interdependence.

Responsibilities requiring collaboration and cooperation are not a good fit. Because helping peers requires time and effort, they note it is not surprising that higher job demands is the critical mechanism leading workaholics away from P-OCB. In their “heroic attempt” to stay on top of their workload, Alessandri et al. note that workaholics fail to perceive the potential rewards associated with P-OCB, such as additional resources, emotional support, and a sense of belonging.

For workaholics, understanding the motivation behind their momentum can help them see the broader range of potential benefits, from professional productivity to personal relationships.

item.title: When "Yes" Means Different Things
item.description:
Cross-Cultural Psychology

When "Yes" Means Different Things

Personal Perspective: What one word taught me about culture and hope.

Posted July 26, 2026

Key points
  • Different cultures may ascribe different meanings to words and languages.
  • Understanding the implicit meaning of words and language can minimize misunderstandings.
  • Yes does not always mean commitment. It maybe a declaration to shape the direction and future.
  • Sometimes saying the word is the first step toward becoming it.

“Can we drive to New Jersey this weekend? I need to get some Japanese supplies “

When I first got married to my American husband, I would ask something like this. I wasn’t driving yet, and getting Japanese stuff was important to a newly arrived immigrant.

“Sure, of course.”

Then the weekend came---we slept in……he had to meet up with his friend……next thing we know, the day was over.

Or I would ask him to get something from the store, while he is running errands. He will say of course, only to forget.

In defense of my husband, he is a very responsible and reliable person, so I am exaggerating rare occurrences. But when these types of things happened, I was not so much disappointed as perplexed.

If he is not 100% sure, why wouldn’t he say something like,

“I am busy during the week with work and probably want to rest this weekend. Driving to New Jersey is a hassle (it is!). I can’t promise so let’s see how the day goes.”

Of course, that does sound a bit robotic and maybe not as romantic for a newlywed.

Over time, I realized my husband wasn't simply being casual. We attached different meanings to the word yes.

Source: donskarpo-iStock

In Japan, our word is our bond. Yes means 100 % commitment. We don’t speak until reality is certain, so in a way, the word “Yes” is a mere confirmation of a future that has happened. For my husband, however, "yes" expressed willingness. It was less a promise than a declaration of intention, and exploration of a possibility.

***

It was not just my husband.

When my friend said,

“I am going back to graduate school”,

I assumed she already got the acceptance letter and was about to start her first class.

“Oh congratulations, when do you start?”

“I have to start carving out some time to study so I can get in.”

From a Japanese sensibility, I would not dare mention such plans until I truly got in. It feels too embarrassing to have declared this and not have gotten in.

article continues after advertisement

But this unease, I have come to realize, was not simply the words and meanings we attached them to. It reflected two different ways of relating to the future.

I began to wonder whether this tendency to declare the future before it exists was part of the American story itself.

In a recent essay in The Atlantic titled American Loneliness, Yari Lapid writes,

"When Thomas Jefferson wrote in the declaration of independence, 'We hold these truths to be self-evidence, that all men are created equal –',

He knew then, and we know now, that America has not perfectly lived up to those words.

Instead, what Jefferson and the founding father were telling the world was: Yes (we know it is not true)—but if we want it badly enough, we can be."

Every culture contains both tendencies, and every person communicates differently so I don’t want to oversimplify the cultural complexity. But this contrast helped me understand one of the biggest misunderstandings in my own marriage.

What my husband was communicating was,

Yes, I will consider you as partner. I will try to consider your needs and wants as part of my life moving forward.

Looking back, I realized my husband was expressing something deeply American—not certainty, but direction.

Similarly, my friend was sharing a tender moment; her goals, future and vulnerability.

***

"Everywhere else in the world, the question that defines people is: Where do you come from?" Lapid writes from the road trips of the vast American land. "In America, it is: Where are you going?"

The Americans escaped from the old rules, and are constaly moving forward. They are trying to get somewhere, even when they may not know where that somewhere is.

In that context, new rules, the new hopes, the new directions are “declared", to make it explicit and to be shared.

The sharing of the vision help decrease our lonliness, even if it is just a tiny bit.

article continues after advertisement

***

We have been married close to 30 years now, so we have gotten use to each other’s communication style.

I still carry some of the rigidity of my Japanese upbringing, and perhaps I always will. But I have learned there is another way to use words. Sometimes they describe reality. Sometimes they help create it. We don't always have to wait until the future is certain before we speak about it. Sometimes saying it is the first step toward becoming it.
